reviewer.notes: Independent AI editorial first pass based only on the blind-review packet. It is not a human signature, rights clearance or publication approval.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Libraries now define success through the practical access they provide, not primarily through the materials they own or lend.
supportingQuotes: measure success differently
The central idea is no longer that the library owns information, but that it gives people practical access to it.

paraphraseMap.mapping: The contrast between owning stored information and enabling people to use spaces, services and information directly paraphrases a shift from ownership to access.

questions.competitorFailure: The database and online-form examples are only two members of a wider list that also includes a desk and a workshop; technology is not the organizing idea of the paragraph.
questions.reasoning: The final sentence states the ownership-versus-access contrast explicitly, so heading vii is only a detail-based distractor. Heading i captures the whole paragraph's explicit shift from ownership to practical access, whereas heading vii covers only selected examples.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Libraries increasingly support neighbourhood residents through learning, employment help and safe public space.
supportingQuotes: libraries have become informal support centers
part of the social infrastructure of a neighborhood

paraphraseMap.mapping: An informal support centre that serves different community groups and provides refuge is a place for community support.

questions.competitorFailure: The services could imply staff involvement, but the paragraph never centres staff or their changing responsibilities; it centres the library's social function.
questions.reasoning: Both the opening claim and concluding generalization point directly to community support. Heading iii covers the paragraph's full range of neighbourhood support functions and its concluding social-infrastructure claim.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Libraries now connect visitors with a wide range of advanced digital help, devices and production tools that may be unaffordable at home.
supportingQuotes: help scanning documents, using design software, joining a video interview or protecting personal data online
makerspaces with recording equipment and 3D printers

paraphraseMap.mapping: Scanning, design software, data protection, device lending and makerspace equipment are technology services substantially broader than basic internet access.

questions.competitorFailure: The final bridge metaphor does concern access, but the paragraph consistently narrows that access to digital services and technology tools; heading i is too general.
questions.reasoning: Heading i captures a secondary access theme, but heading vii accounts for the full chain of examples and the opening topic sentence. Heading vii accounts for the opening change in visitor needs and the entire sequence of advanced digital services, devices and makerspace tools.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Library employees now combine traditional collection work with teaching, technical support, partnership coordination and online guidance.
supportingQuotes: These changes have also transformed library work.
Staff members still organize collections, but they may also teach classes, troubleshoot devices, coordinate local partnerships and guide users through government websites.

paraphraseMap.mapping: The still-but-also contrast explicitly describes a widening set of staff responsibilities and the additional skills those duties require.

questions.competitorFailure: Teaching and government-site guidance support users, but they are examples used to demonstrate changes in staff work, not a description of the library's overall community role.
questions.reasoning: The paragraph's grammatical subject and conclusion are both staff work and staff skills. Heading v matches the paragraph's explicit transformation of library work, from traditional collection duties to multiple new roles and skills.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Library use shows simultaneous decline in some traditional activity and growth in other services, a mixed result obscured by borrowing-based measures.
supportingQuotes: usage patterns are more complex
Traditional book borrowing has decreased in some places, yet attendance at events, demand for study areas and use of digital services have grown.
older measures

paraphraseMap.mapping: The decrease-yet-growth contrast is the mixed pattern, while funders' continued reliance on traditional indicators explains how older measures miss it.

questions.competitorFailure: The paragraph explicitly rejects a decline-only interpretation by setting reduced borrowing against growth in attendance, study-space demand and digital use.
questions.reasoning: Heading viii is contradicted by the evidence; the paragraph explicitly names the picture as mixed. Heading ix captures both the mixed decline-and-growth evidence and the concluding warning that older metrics fail to represent it.

passageAssessment.notes: The title signals general change but does not disclose which distinct change belongs to any one paragraph. The set tests whole-paragraph matching cleanly and all mappings are unique, but explicit topic sentences, a near one-to-one thematic sequence and extreme distractors such as complete disappearance, unlimited opening hours and only declining make it easier than a typical high-discrimination IELTS set. No paragraph has material heading ambiguity when judged by its whole-paragraph main idea.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Urban growers respond to scarce open land by turning small, overlooked urban sites into productive spaces.
supportingQuotes: cities have little unused land
organisers use rooftops, school courtyards, vacant lots and narrow strips beside public buildings

paraphraseMap.mapping: Using rooftops and other small, unconventional sites is the project's practical response to limited urban land.

questions.competitorFailure: The sentence about harvest size concedes a limitation but introduces no debate about evaluation; the paragraph is organized around finding space.
questions.reasoning: Low yields are subordinate to the explicit opening problem of scarce land and the list of spatial adaptations. Heading i covers the explicit space constraint, the alternative sites used in response and the concluding transformation of overlooked corners.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Producing food near consumers can reduce transport, packaging and landfill waste.
supportingQuotes: environmental value of growing food close to consumers
require less transport and packaging
reduce the amount of organic waste sent to landfill

paraphraseMap.mapping: Local production shortens the route from grower to consumer, yielding the stated environmental benefits in transport, packaging and waste.

questions.competitorFailure: Physical proximity is mentioned, but no shortage of land or adaptation of space appears; proximity is used to explain environmental impact.
questions.reasoning: The environmental frame is explicit and covers both the tomato example and composting. Heading vii unifies the local-food transport example and the connected composting benefit under the paragraph's explicit environmental frame.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: School gardens work as cross-curricular classrooms for science, writing, food knowledge and citizenship rather than as isolated gardening activities.
supportingQuotes: gardens can become outdoor classrooms
supports science, language and citizenship lessons rather than sitting outside the curriculum

paraphraseMap.mapping: The garden's value extends from growing plants into several academic and civic learning domains.

questions.competitorFailure: Citizenship lessons may concern community life, but the paragraph says nothing about resident ownership, trust or shared project rules.
questions.reasoning: Every example is an educational use and the conclusion explicitly integrates the garden into the curriculum. Heading iii captures the outdoor-classroom frame, the varied learning activities and the conclusion that gardens should support multiple curriculum areas.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Urban gardens are more durable when residents help make decisions and consequently feel responsible for the project.
supportingQuotes: more likely to last when residents feel they have shaped the rules
Shared decisions about opening hours, crop choices and maintenance can create a stronger sense of responsibility.

paraphraseMap.mapping: Listening to neighbours and sharing decisions establish local ownership and trust, which the paragraph links to durability and responsibility.

questions.competitorFailure: Maintenance responsibility might involve voluntary effort, but volunteers and risks arising from their use are never discussed.
questions.reasoning: The outside-organization contrast and repeated emphasis on residents' decisions directly support heading iv. Heading iv explains the full causal sequence: resident participation produces ownership and responsibility, which makes the project more durable.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Crop weight alone undervalues small urban farms because their education, social and demonstration benefits may matter even when output is modest.
supportingQuotes: counting kilograms of produce
Critics argue that this can miss the point.
yet it may still provide education, social connection and visible evidence that food systems can be changed locally

paraphraseMap.mapping: The supporters-versus-critics structure directly debates yield as a measure and supplies several non-yield outcomes that a narrow metric misses.

questions.competitorFailure: Education is only one of three alternative benefits listed; the larger point is that yield should not be the sole standard of success.
questions.reasoning: Heading iii captures one supporting detail, whereas heading viii captures the explicit evaluative debate and all examples. Heading viii matches the explicit dispute over kilograms as a success measure and embraces all three alternative benefits in the conclusion.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Contamination, structural capacity and water constraints mean urban farms need testing, permission and maintenance planning.
supportingQuotes: There are also practical limits.
Soil may be contaminated, roofs may not support heavy containers, and water access can be unreliable in summer.
start with testing, permissions and maintenance plans

paraphraseMap.mapping: The physical constraints are technical limits, and the prescribed tests, approvals and maintenance arrangements constitute realistic planning.

questions.competitorFailure: The warning that enthusiasm is insufficient might superficially suggest volunteer risk, but no volunteer model is mentioned and all stated obstacles are site or infrastructure constraints.
questions.reasoning: The heading mirrors both halves of the paragraph: practical constraints followed by planning responses. Heading v precisely covers the paragraph's structure: three practical constraints followed by the testing, permissions and plans needed to address them.

passageAssessment.notes: Beyond fresh food previews the set's repeated non-yield benefits and especially supports Paragraph E, although it does not determine the other five matches. The six headings form a coherent formative set and require some whole-paragraph discrimination, especially in Paragraphs A and E. However, explicit topic sentences, transparent lexical paraphrases and implausible absolute distractors reduce the difficulty below a typical live IELTS Matching Headings task. No material ambiguity remains; secondary themes in Paragraphs A, C and E are narrower than the selected whole-paragraph headings.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Previously reduced night-train services are being revived because some travellers now value lower-emission travel and avoiding early airport transfers.
supportingQuotes: Recently, several operators have announced new overnight services.
The revival reflects a shift in passenger priorities

paraphraseMap.mapping: New overnight routes are the revived service, and the newly valued environmental and convenience benefits are the changing priorities behind it.

questions.competitorFailure: Lower emissions are one reason for the revival, but the paragraph also emphasizes avoiding early airport transfers and frames both as a broader shift in priorities.
questions.reasoning: Heading vi fits one substantial detail, but heading i uniquely covers the decline-revival history and both stated passenger priorities. Heading i uniquely covers the paragraph's complete decline-to-revival arc and both environmental and convenience changes in passenger priorities.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Night trains appeal to lower-impact travellers because their carbon emissions can be far below those of equivalent flights.
supportingQuotes: compare night trains with flights in terms of carbon emissions
A rail journey can produce far less pollution than a plane on the same route
this difference is a major part of the appeal

paraphraseMap.mapping: The lower-emissions comparison is the environmental argument, and its role in passenger appeal explains renewed interest.

questions.competitorFailure: Reduced-footprint travel is a changing priority, but this paragraph does not discuss the service's disappearance and revival; it develops the environmental case alone.
questions.reasoning: The paragraph's exclusive focus on carbon and pollution makes heading vi more precise than the broader heading i. Heading vi accounts for the complete flight-versus-rail emissions comparison and the conclusion that this environmental difference drives passenger appeal.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Overnight trains crossing national rail systems require difficult coordination because rules, maintenance windows, signalling and delays interact across borders.
supportingQuotes: Trains may cross several national networks
each with its own track access rules, maintenance windows and signalling systems
A delay in one country can also affect morning commuter services in another

paraphraseMap.mapping: Maintenance windows and delays affecting other scheduled services are timetabling problems, and the multiple national networks make them cross-border challenges.

questions.competitorFailure: The paragraph concerns the operational feasibility of a route, not passenger priorities or why the service has returned.
questions.reasoning: Heading iv directly unifies every operational example; no other heading covers international scheduling coordination. Heading iv unifies the national-network rules, maintenance windows, signalling differences and cross-border delay consequences as one coordination problem.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Operators must balance different passenger expectations for overnight comfort against the capacity consequences of each accommodation type.
supportingQuotes: Passenger expectations can be difficult to balance.
Some people imagine a hotel-like cabin, while others mainly want a clean, safe place to sleep.
each choice affects both comfort and capacity

paraphraseMap.mapping: The competing visions of accommodation are comfort expectations, while choosing the mix of compartments, couchettes and seats is how operators manage them.

questions.competitorFailure: Capacity can affect commercial outcomes, but the paragraph neither mentions prices nor identifies affordability or access by customer group; it focuses on comfort and capacity design.
questions.reasoning: The opening and closing sentences explicitly frame the issue as balancing comfort expectations. Heading iii captures the contrasting comfort expectations and the operator's resulting need to choose an accommodation mix that balances comfort with capacity.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Night-train pricing must reconcile affordability for families and students with the operator's need to cover substantial service costs.
supportingQuotes: If a sleeper ticket costs much more than a flight, families and students may not see it as a realistic option.
Subsidies, early-booking fares and shared compartments can help
operators still need enough revenue to cover staff, cleaning and rolling stock

paraphraseMap.mapping: The paragraph connects ticket price to access for particular travellers and weighs price-reduction mechanisms against financial viability.

questions.competitorFailure: Shared compartments and cleaning touch on the travel experience, but they appear as pricing or cost variables; no competing comfort expectations are discussed.
questions.reasoning: Price is named as the obstacle and both passenger affordability and operator revenue are developed around it. Heading viii covers both sides of the paragraph's pricing problem: whether key passenger groups can afford the service and whether operators can cover its costs.

questions.mainIdeaStatement: Advertising reframes overnight rail travel as an enjoyable and meaningful part of a holiday rather than merely transport between destinations.
supportingQuotes: Marketing teams increasingly present the overnight journey as more than transport.
This message turns the train into part of the holiday rather than a pause before it begins.

paraphraseMap.mapping: Presenting the ride as more than transport and as part of the holiday is marketing the journey itself as part of the trip.

questions.competitorFailure: The campaign may respond to traveller preferences, but the paragraph does not explain the service's revival; it describes a specific promotional framing.
questions.reasoning: The heading is effectively a concise paraphrase of both the opening claim and final sentence. Heading ix directly paraphrases the opening marketing claim, the advertisement example and the final redefinition of the train as part of the holiday.

passageAssessment.notes: The title directly previews Paragraph A's return/revival concept and makes heading i unusually easy there, although it does not resolve Paragraphs B-F. The set has clear, unique paragraph functions and a useful local contrast between headings i and vi. It is nevertheless easier than a typical live IELTS set because most headings closely echo topic sentences, several alternatives make unsupported absolute claims, and the passage title strongly cues Paragraph A. No material ambiguity remains. Paragraph A has the closest competition, but heading i covers the full revival-and-priorities frame whereas heading vi covers only its emissions detail.
